# Continual-ARC notes: noisy axis-aligned rectangles (task-a130a2b4)

This instance ended unsolved after 8 wrong submissions. Keep this as a hypothesis/playbook for future similar tasks, not as a verified solution.

## Evidence from demos

Both demonstrations show an image with a uniform background, many axis-aligned solid rectangular objects in assorted colors (including objects in the demo's color 0), and isolated pixels of other colors that act as corruption. The output removes those stray pixels (replacing them with background) and repairs corruptions inside rectangle objects so the rectangles become solid again.

- Demo 1: background 7; the 2 and 6 rectangles are retained/repaired; scattered 3/5/8 noise disappears. The 2x5-ish block at rows 5-7, cols 0-4 stays as 6 where present, with a 3 speck removed; central rectangles of 2 are completed through 5-noise.
- Demo 2: background 4; solid rectangles (colors 0, 3, 8) are retained and restored, while outlier pixels 2 and 6 disappear. The 0 rectangles are objects because the background is 4.

Likely operation: identify each intended solid rectangle; fill its bounding rectangle in its object's original color; set isolated corruption pixels to the background. Treat all palette colors as possible object colors; do not assume a fixed noise color or that 0 is always background.

## Why the task-a130a2b4 attempts likely failed

I tried manually listing rectangular objects and outputting reconstructed rectangles with 6-noise removed. All eight submissions were incorrect; none of the candidate grids is verified. Avoid blindly reusing them.

Likely weak point: inferring which corrupted pixels belong to which object / whether rectangles can be recovered by connected components alone. A 6 corruption can disconnect or border a shape, and independent adjacent rectangles may share colors. Carefully use whole-grid alignment and all noisy cells; preserve any genuine pixel not identified as noise. Make a complete per-cell audit against input before submit.

In future, use demonstrations to establish the rule, then carefully re-evaluate any apparent rectangle touching/overlapping or interrupted by noise. Don't spend attempts on speculative repeated variants.
